title: Are all these RUST rebuilds way more optimized?
author: credible_human
selftext: You've probably seen the videos of people mixing 2 games together like dark souls x Minecraft. The way I've heard it was done is they convert both games to RUST and then it's way easier to mash them together. What I'm wondering is: do they perform much better in RUST? Could we take horribly optimized games , convert them to RUST and then be able to play them on shittier hardware?

comments.author: matteo101man
comments.body:
To answer your question from someone who actually did a RUST recomp, yes. Majority of people using RUST are using the BEVY engine, which has all the freedom of expression as pretty much any other game engine.

You can employ optimization methods like lods, frustum&occlusion culling etc, I mean you're genuinely having to rewrite code to port over an entire game, so you can put in whatever you want; I even added super resolution to the one I was working on.

The limit is just how much someone actually wants to optimize the game.

comments.author: TechgeekOne
comments.body:
No, it's a lot more nuanced than that. The language used just makes certain things easier or harder, and some have an inherent cost depending on where they sit in the abstraction hierarchy. 

So for example if you took pure Python code for example (not python calling C, plain interpreted python) and translated it to Rust then yes, the Rust version would be faster. But if you took well written C++ and translated it to Rust I'd expect roughly equal performance between them because they work at a similar level of abstraction. 

But it gets messier than that because how the code is written matters too. You can write the same thing in Python and Rust and if the python one manages it's memory in a more machine friendly data oriented way it will be faster than the Rust code despite Python being "slower". 

Basically the language itself doesn't matter all that much except for how easily you can express something and control the physical machine itself. The way the code uses said machine is what matters the most for performance.

comments.author: Weaves87
comments.body:
That's not how it works.

Rust is a memory-safe, high performance systems programming language (also happens to be my fave language as a long time dev) but just converting something to Rust is not going to unlock some kind of crazy performance benefit in your game.

If anything, it will probably create significantly more technical debt because you're having to rewrite a lot of functionality that is already implemented in Unity, Unreal, or Godot in Rust.

All the major engines are fast enough to create ridiculously highly optimized games. If they weren't, you would see AAA game studios investing their time elsewhere.

Occasionally you will find games with completely custom built engines, but they are almost certainly doing something that is very highly specialized (e.g. Factorio a good example). Remixing a few games together isn't something that requires it

replies.author: credible_human
replies.body:
>all the major engines are fast enough to create ridiculously highly optimized games

This could be true but there are many examples of the latest unreal engine games that are horribly optimized. Oblivions remaster is a good example, can't even hit 60fps on modern gen consoles. That could be the devs fault, sure, but how long have they had to fix the optimization issues but haven't? It's been more than a year, maybe longer.

replies.author: Weaves87
replies.body:
In that particular example, the graphics are built on Unreal but they also run the original engine and game at the same time (for quests, etc): there’s just some interprocess communication at play that dramatically decreases performance. You’re running 2 games at the same time

The main point is that this is not necessarily an Unreal problem. It’s an engineering problem and tradeoff that Bethesda decided to just run with
